title: Longest calm stretch
statement:
A sensor records one reading per second as a string of lowercase letters, one letter per reading. A stretch is calm if no letter repeats inside it.

Return the length of the longest calm stretch of consecutive readings.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the input only lowercase letters?
clarifyingQuestions.why: Means the window holds at most 26 distinct letters, which bounds the extra space.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should an empty string return?
Do the readings in a stretch have to be consecutive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, a stretch is a run of consecutive readings.
clarifyingQuestions.why: Distinguishes this from picking any subset of letters.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How long can the string be?

hiddenConstraints: Only lowercase letters a to z.

edgeCases.why: Every letter repeats immediately; the answer is 1.
When the second a arrives, its last position is before the window start; jumping back would be a bug.
No repeats at all; the whole string is the answer.

approaches.name: Check every substring
approaches.idea: For every start and end, check whether the substring has a repeated letter.
approaches.time: O(n^3), or O(n^2) with a set per start
approaches.tradeoffs: Easy to reason about but far too slow at 100,000 readings.

approaches.name: Sliding window with a set
approaches.idea: Grow the right edge; while the new letter is already in the window, remove letters from the left. Track the largest window.
approaches.tradeoffs: Each letter enters and leaves the window at most once.

approaches.name: Sliding window with last-seen positions
approaches.idea: Store each letter’s last position. When a letter repeats inside the window, move the left edge to just after its previous position in one jump.
approaches.tradeoffs: Same complexity as the set version but skips the inner loop; needs care so the left edge never moves backward.

optimal.name: Sliding window with last-seen positions
optimal.explanation: Keep start, the left edge of the current calm window, and last, a map from letter to its most recent position. For each position i with letter c: if c was seen at a position at or after start, move start to that position plus one. Record last[c] = i and update best with i - start + 1.

hintLadder: If a stretch from i to j is calm, what do you know about the stretch from i to j minus one?
Can you reuse work as you extend the stretch by one reading instead of starting over?
Think of a window with a left and right edge. When should the left edge move?
Keep each letter’s last position. When the new letter was last seen inside the window, move the left edge just past it.

walkthrough.say: Just lowercase letters? And for an empty string I return zero, right? The stretch has to be consecutive readings, not any subset?
Brute force would check every substring for repeats, which is at least n squared. With a hundred thousand readings that’s too slow.

Instead I’ll keep a window that is always calm. I extend the right edge one reading at a time, and when the new letter is already inside the window, I move the left edge just past its previous position. Each step is constant work, so O(n) time, and the map only ever holds 26 letters.
I need the window start, the best length so far, and each letter’s last position.
Here’s the subtle part. I only move start if the previous position is inside the current window, otherwise start could jump backward.

Let me trace a, b, b, a. At index 2 the second b was last seen at 1, which is in the window, so start becomes 2. At index 3, a was last seen at 0, which is before start, so start stays 2. The window is b, a, length 2. Without that check start would have gone back to 1.

Now beeper. b, e gives a window of 2. At index 2 the e repeats, so start moves to 2. At index 4 another e, last seen at 2, so start moves to 3. Then r makes the window p, e, r, length 3, which matches the example.
O(n) time and constant extra space because the alphabet is fixed. For Unicode, the map would grow with the number of distinct characters.
